JLBind is the Julia package your binding package uses to talk to R.
`using JLBind` gives you `@rcall`, `@narrow`, `from_sexp`, `to_sexp`, `SEXP`,
`RRef`, `RVector` and `RDataFrame`; use the rest as `JLBind.name`.

## Declaring entrypoints

### `@rcall` {#macro-rcall}

```julia
@rcall f(arg::T, ...)::R
```

Make `f` callable from R. `jlbind::update_entrypoints()` writes a matching R
function for each `@rcall`.

```julia
greet(name) = "Hello, " * name * "!"

@rcall greet(name::String)::String
```

Every argument and the return value need a type, which decides how they are
converted (see [`from_sexp`](#from_sexp) and [`to_sexp`](#to_sexp)). Use
[`RRef{T}`](#rref) to give R a Julia object by reference. An argument of type
`Union{Nothing,T}` accepts `NULL`, and `Union{Missing,T}` accepts `NA`.

An argument can have a default, which the R function gets too: a number, string,
`true`, `false`, `missing` (`NA`), `nothing` (`NULL`), or a vector of these such
as `[1, 2]`.

If `f` throws, R gets an error. The message of an `ArgumentError`, `error()` and
a few other common exceptions is passed on; others get a generic message.

Write each `@rcall` at the top level of a file, as `update_entrypoints()` reads
the source.

## Converting values

`@rcall` converts arguments and return values with these.

### `from_sexp` {#from_sexp}

```julia
from_sexp(T, x::SEXP) -> T
```

Convert the R object `x` to a `T`, or throw an `ArgumentError` saying what was
expected. `@rcall` converts every argument with it; add a method to accept a
type of your own.

It supports:

- `String` and `Symbol` (from a string or factor), `Bool`, `Float64`, `Int64`,
  `Int32`, `ComplexF64`, `Date`, `DateTime` and the smaller number types, and
  vectors of all of these;
- `Union{Missing,T}` and `Vector{Union{Missing,T}}`, which allow `NA`;
- `Union{Nothing,T}`, which allows `NULL`;
- `Matrix{T}` and `Array{T,N}`, from an R matrix or array;
- other `Vector`s, `Tuple`s, `NamedTuple`s and `Dict{String,T}`, from a list;
- [`RVector{T}`](#rvector), [`RDataFrame`](#rdataframe), and `SEXP`, which is
  passed as is.

### `to_sexp` {#to_sexp}

```julia
to_sexp(x) -> SEXP
```

Convert `x` to an R object. `@rcall` converts every return value with it; add a
method to return a type of your own.

It supports the types [`from_sexp`](#from_sexp) does, plus `nothing` (`NULL`)
and `missing` (`NA`). An `Int64` becomes a double, since R's integers have 32
bits: return an `Int32` for an R integer.

### `RVector` {#rvector}

```julia
RVector{T}
```

A read-only view of the data of an R vector, without a copy: `RVector{Float64}`
for a double vector, `RVector{Int32}` for an integer vector and `RVector{UInt8}`
for a raw vector. Use it for a large vector you only read.

`NA` is not checked for, and the view is only valid during the call, so don't
keep it. Returning it returns the R vector it views.

### `RDataFrame` {#rdataframe}

```julia
RDataFrame(columns::NamedTuple)
```

A data frame, converted to and from an R `data.frame` (or tibble). Its columns
are `df.x` and so on. As an argument, the data frame must have exactly these
columns, in any order.

```julia
const Sales = RDataFrame{(:group, :amount),Tuple{Vector{String},Vector{Float64}}}

total(df) = sum(df.amount)

@rcall total(df::Sales)::Float64
```

## Julia objects in R

### `RRef` {#rref}

```julia
RRef{T}
```

A Julia object that R holds by reference, for objects that are easier to keep in
Julia than to convert:

```julia
new_counter(start) = Counter(start)
increment(c, by) = (c.n += by; c.n)

@rcall new_counter(start::Int64)::RRef{Counter}
@rcall increment(c::RRef{Counter}, by::Int64)::Int64
```

R gets an object of class [`r_class(T)`](#r_class) that it can pass back to any
entrypoint taking an `RRef{T}`, and a `Vector{RRef{T}}` is a list of them. The
Julia object is freed once R no longer uses it. A reference that is saved and
loaded again has lost its object, unless the type supports saving (see
[`r_saved_by`](#r_saved_by)).

If `T` is abstract, take the argument with `@nospecialize` and call methods on
it with [`@narrow`](#macro-narrow).

### `r_class` {#r_class}

```julia
r_class(T) -> String
```

The R class of references to `T`s, `"jlbind_ref"` by default. Define a method to
give them a class of their own, for methods such as `print()`:

```julia
JLBind.r_class(::Type{Model}) = "mymodel"
```

### `r_saved_by` {#r_saved_by}

```julia
r_saved_by(T) -> Union{String,Nothing}
```

Return your package's name to let references to `T`s be saved with `saveRDS()`
and the like. By default they can't be: a reference that is saved and loaded
again has lost its object.

Saving also needs an [`r_restore`](#r_restore) method, and an R function
`.jlbind_saved_state(x)` in your package (it need not be exported) that returns
a list to rebuild the object from:

```julia
JLBind.r_saved_by(::Type{Model}) = "mypackage"
JLBind.r_restore(::Type{Model}, state::SEXP) =
    Model(from_sexp(NamedTuple{(:weights,),Tuple{Vector{Float64}}}, state).weights)
```

```r
.jlbind_saved_state <- function(x) list(weights = model_weights(x))
```

The object is rebuilt the first time a loaded reference is used. Supporting
saving adds about 400 ns to creating each reference, and `saveRDS(version = 2)`
can't save one.

### `r_restore` {#r_restore}

```julia
r_restore(T, state::SEXP) -> T
```

Rebuild a `T` from the list `.jlbind_saved_state()` returned when it was saved
(see [`r_saved_by`](#r_saved_by)). The list may come from an older version of
your package, so check any version it records.

### `object_count` {#object_count}

```julia
object_count() -> Int64
```

How many Julia objects R holds references to, to check that they are freed.

## Trimming

### `@narrow` {#macro-narrow}

```julia
@narrow x (A, B, ...) expr [otherwise]
```

Evaluate `expr` with `x` known to be an `A`, a `B`, and so on, whichever it is.
If it is none of them, evaluate `otherwise`, or throw an `ArgumentError`.

The compiled library needs this to call methods on an argument of an abstract
type:

```julia
shape_area(@nospecialize(s::Shape)) = @narrow s (Circle, Square) area(s)
```

## Building R objects

To build a result yourself, without a copy, declare the entrypoint to return
`SEXP` and use these, which call R's C API directly. Most don't check their
arguments, so a wrong type or index crashes R instead of giving an error.

### `SEXP` {#sexp}

```julia
SEXP
```

An R object, as R's C API passes it. Declare an entrypoint to return `SEXP` to
build its result yourself.

### `@R` {#macro-r}

```julia
@R(name)
```

A function or variable of R's C API, for `ccall` or `cglobal`:

```julia
ccall(@R(Rf_xlength), Int, (SEXP,), x)
```

### `@r_global` {#macro-r_global}

```julia
@r_global(name)
```

The value of one of R's global `SEXP` variables, such as
`@r_global(R_NaString)`.

### `nil` {#nil}

```julia
nil() -> SEXP
```

R's `NULL`.

### `rtypeof`, `rlength` {#rtypeof}

```julia
rtypeof(x::SEXP) -> Cint
rlength(x::SEXP) -> Int
```

The type of `x` (such as [`REALSXP`](#nilsxp)), and its length.

### `NILSXP`, `LGLSXP`, `INTSXP`, `REALSXP`, `CPLXSXP`, `STRSXP`, `VECSXP`, `EXTPTRSXP`, `RAWSXP` {#nilsxp}

```julia
NILSXP, LGLSXP, INTSXP, REALSXP, CPLXSXP, STRSXP, VECSXP, EXTPTRSXP, RAWSXP
```

R's object types, as [`rtypeof`](#rtypeof) returns them and [`alloc`](#alloc)
takes them: `NULL`, logical, integer, double, complex, character and raw
vectors, a list, and an external pointer.

### `NA_INTEGER`, `NA_REAL` {#na_integer}

```julia
NA_INTEGER, NA_REAL
```

R's `NA` in an integer or logical vector, and in a double vector.

### `protect`, `unprotect` {#protect}

```julia
protect(x::SEXP) -> x
unprotect(n)
```

Keep `x` from R's garbage collector while you allocate other R objects, and
release the last `n` objects protected, before returning. These are R's
`PROTECT` and `UNPROTECT`.

### `preserve`, `release` {#preserve}

```julia
preserve(x::SEXP) -> x
release(x::SEXP)
```

Keep `x` alive across calls, until it is released.

### `alloc`, `alloc_matrix` {#alloc}

```julia
alloc(t, n) -> SEXP
alloc_matrix(t, nrow, ncol) -> SEXP
```

A new R vector of type `t` and length `n`, or matrix of `nrow` rows and `ncol`
columns, to fill in. [`protect`](#protect) it before allocating anything else.

### `mkchar` {#mkchar}

```julia
mkchar(s::Union{String,Symbol}) -> SEXP
```

An R string, the element of a character vector. Strings of symbols are cached,
which makes returning many names faster.

### `string_elt`, `set_string_elt`, `vector_elt`, `set_vector_elt` {#string_elt}

```julia
string_elt(x::SEXP, i) -> SEXP
set_string_elt(x::SEXP, i, v::SEXP)
vector_elt(x::SEXP, i) -> SEXP
set_vector_elt(x::SEXP, i, v::SEXP)
```

Get and set element `i` of a character vector or list. Indices start at 0, as in
C, and aren't checked. Make an element of a character vector with
[`mkchar`](#mkchar).

### `real_ptr`, `int_ptr`, `logical_ptr`, `complex_ptr`, `raw_ptr` {#real_ptr}

```julia
real_ptr(x::SEXP) -> Ptr{Float64}
int_ptr(x::SEXP) -> Ptr{Cint}
logical_ptr(x::SEXP) -> Ptr{Cint}
complex_ptr(x::SEXP) -> Ptr{ComplexF64}
raw_ptr(x::SEXP) -> Ptr{UInt8}
```

A pointer to the data of a double, integer, logical, complex or raw vector, to
read with `unsafe_load` or fill with `unsafe_store!`. The type of `x` isn't
checked.

### `get_attrib`, `set_attrib` {#get_attrib}

```julia
get_attrib(x::SEXP, name::SEXP) -> SEXP
set_attrib(x::SEXP, name::SEXP, value::SEXP)
```

Get and set the attribute `name` of `x`, where `name` is an R symbol such as
`@r_global(R_NamesSymbol)`. A missing attribute is `NULL`.

### `data_frame` {#data_frame}

```julia
data_frame(names::Vector{String}, columns::Vector{SEXP}) -> SEXP
```

An R `data.frame` of the R vectors `columns`, for columns whose types are only
known at run time. Keep the columns protected until the call returns. When the
types are known, return an [`RDataFrame`](#rdataframe) instead.
